new_statements.rule_in_words: Survey-wide note by the fieldworker for all Lumi-Subdistrict languages he recorded (Seta = no. 2, informant Kutek of Pelama, June 1967): stress is not phonemic; by default it falls on the first syllable whose vowel is not schwa, and is written only when it falls elsewhere. In his 46-item Seta list (as re-keyed on TransNewGuinea) only kamóya 'bone' is marked non-initial; the rest (pənaluwa, pəsiapa, təpəli, naməna, awute, sakul...) are unmarked, i.e. initial / first-full-vowel stress.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated in prose; one lexical item in the Seta list marked with second-syllable stress (kamóya 'bone').
new_statements.domain_note: Isolated citation forms in a survey wordlist; statement is a transcription convention plus a non-phonemic verdict applying to c. 40 languages at once, not a Seta-specific description. 'First syllable not containing schwa' could equally be read as leftmost-full-vowel (schwa syllables unstressable). scanned of the snippet prints the schwa symbol as [a]. Note that for the closely related One (Molmo), Donohue later reported penultimate stress with lexical contrasts in verbs, so Laycock's blanket verdict is shallow.
new_statements.identity_note: Laycock's 1968 Seta data = villages Merabu and Pelama, informant Kutek of Pelama (matches Glottolog seta1245 / ISO stf, alt. name Aunalei, shared with Seti [sbi, seti1248] and One). Laycock 1973 notes Seti 'could be regarded as a dialect of' Seta. The stress remark is not Seta-specific: it is a blanket note over all c. 40 Lumi-Subdistrict survey languages.
